name: DAC7513N_3K
title: DAC7513: single 12-bit voltage-output DAC with 3-wire serial input, 2.7 V to 5.5 V, SOT23-8 and MSOP-8
summary: A single-channel 12-bit string DAC whose buffered output swings from rail to rail. Full scale is set by an external reference applied at VREF, which may be anywhere from 0 V up to VDD, so the part can also work as a multiplier. Codes arrive as 16-bit words over SYNC, SCLK and DIN at up to 30 MHz. The output comes up at 0 V after power is applied, and two control bits select normal operation or one of three power-down states in which the output is grounded through 1 kΩ, through 100 kΩ, or left open. It draws 115 µA typical at 5 V and 0.2 µA typical when powered down. DAC7513N/3K is the SOT23-8 part on a 3000-piece reel.

circuits.title: REF02 as the supply for the DAC7513
circuits.description: A REF02 running from +15 V makes a precise 5 V rail and that rail powers the DAC, so the converter sees a quiet supply even where the system rails are noisy or are not 5 V. With no load on VOUT the DAC takes 132 µA (IDD plus IREF) from the REF02; any output load current comes from the REF02 as well. The output spans 0 V to 5 V and the DAC is written over SYNC, SCLK and DIN.
notes: The REF02 rail carries IDD plus IREF (132 µA), so it feeds VREF as well as VDD; VFB joins VOUT.

circuits.title: Bipolar output with an OPA703
circuits.description: An OPA703 on ±5 V turns the unipolar DAC output into a ±VREF swing. VFB and VOUT are tied together and drive the amplifier's non-inverting input. R1 runs from the reference node to the inverting input and R2 from there to the amplifier output, so the gain from the DAC is (R1 + R2)/R1 and VREF × R2/R1 is subtracted. With VREF = 5 V and R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ, code 000H gives -5 V and FFFH gives +5 V. 10 µF and 0.1 µF decouple the reference node.
notes: With VREF = 2.5 V the same circuit gives ±2.5 V.

operation.text: A resistor string between REF(+) and REF(-) (ground) feeds an output buffer amplifier. The string is a chain of equal resistors R; the code picks one tap, and closing that tap's switch connects it to the amplifier. Being a string, the converter is monotonic by construction.
The buffer swings from 0 V to VDD and can drive 2 kΩ in parallel with 1000 pF to ground. Slew rate is 1 V/µs; half-scale settling with no load is 8 µs.
VFB is the amplifier's inverting input brought out to a pin. Joining VFB to VOUT right at the load improves accuracy, and other conditioning circuitry may be placed between the two pins.

Three wires, SYNC, SCLK and DIN, compatible with SPI, QSPI and Microwire and with most DSPs. A falling SYNC opens a frame; each falling SCLK edge, at up to 30 MHz, shifts one DIN bit into the 16-bit register, and the 16th edge applies the new code and/or mode. After that SYNC can be left low or raised, but a new frame needs a falling SYNC edge after at least 33 ns high. SYNC high costs more input-buffer current than SYNC low, so the lowest-power idle state is SYNC low, raised just before the next frame.
16 bits, MSB first: two don't-care bits, then PD1 and PD0 selecting the operating mode, then the 12 data bits D11 to D0. All 16 move to the DAC on the 16th falling SCLK edge.

In a normal frame SYNC stays low for at least 16 falling SCLK edges and the DAC updates on the 16th. If SYNC goes high before the 16th edge the frame is abandoned: the shift register resets and neither the DAC register nor the mode changes.
At power-up the DAC register is cleared to zero, so the output starts at 0 V and holds there until the first valid write.

PD1 = PD0 = 0 is normal operation at 115 µA typical at 5 V. The other three settings are power-down modes in which supply current falls to 200 nA at 5 V (50 nA at 3 V), all linear circuitry stops, and the output pin is switched from the amplifier to a known termination: 1 kΩ to GND, 100 kΩ to GND, or open (High-Z). The DAC register keeps its contents in power-down. Returning to normal mode takes 2.5 µs typical at VDD = 5 V and 5 µs at VDD = 3 V.

TXD drives SCLK, RXD drives DIN and port pin P3.3 drives SYNC. P3.3 goes low, the 8051 sends one byte (eight falling clock edges), P3.3 stays low while a second byte is sent, and P3.3 goes high after it. The 8051 sends its serial data LSB first while the DAC expects MSB first, so the software must reverse the bit order.
The Microwire device shifts data out on the falling edge of SK, and the DAC takes each bit in on the rising edge of SK.

SCK drives SCLK, MOSI drives DIN and port line PC7 drives SYNC. Set CPOL = 0 and CPHA = 1 so data on MOSI is valid at the falling SCK edge. PC7 goes low, two 8-bit transfers are made MSB first with PC7 held low between them, and PC7 goes high at the end.

Because the DAC needs so little current, a REF02 +5 V reference can serve as its supply, which helps where the system supply is noisy or is not 5 V. The REF02 supplies 132 µA to the unloaded DAC plus whatever the output load draws.

Digital and analog return currents all leave through the one GND pin. Connect GND straight to an analog ground plane kept apart from the digital ground until the two join at the system's power-entry point. More digital logic, and faster switching, near the converter make good performance harder to reach.

VDD should be well regulated and quiet; switching regulators and digital logic put high-frequency spikes on supply rails. Supply noise reaches the output only when the supply is also used as the reference. Run VDD on its own +5 V plane or trace, joined to the digital supply only at the power-entry point, and fit 1 µF to 10 µF plus 0.1 µF bypass capacitors. Further filtering, such as a 100 µF electrolytic or an LC pi filter, may be needed to remove high-frequency noise from the supply.
